💡 Key Takeaways
  • The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) stated in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated.".
  • It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward.".
  • Shortly after Russia debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) stated in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated.".

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward.".

Shortly after Russia debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence.".

Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

According to recent reports, two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.

On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there.".

Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship.".

In a statement to DW on Wednesday, a German government spokesperson reiterated Berlin's position on the matter from the weekend, saying it viewed Friday's CAS ruling "very critically.".

The spokesperson also said  the government would "consult with the German Ice Hockey Federation in the near future regarding the potential consequences of this decision, including its impact on the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany.".

Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.

This came shortly after Norway mentioned it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.

Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.

Latvia's federation mentioned it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.

Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia.".

USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

It has been revealed that "We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

On Wednesday afternoon, yet another sponsor joined the list, with German workwear company Strauss saying it would "forgo all logo exposure associated with the (men's) tournament" and was considering withdrawing its sponsporship entirely.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

Sources indicate that this article was originally published on November 4, 2026. It was updated on November 5, 2026 with the German government statement to DW.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing footballer Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.
  • Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool Magistrates' Court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the opening match of the Premier League season at Anfield on August 15 last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 05:49 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 08:12 EST, 20 November 2026.

A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing footballer Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.

Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool Magistrates' Court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the opening match of the Premier League season at Anfield on August 15 last year.

But Simon Jones, prosecuting, remarked: 'Following recent contact made with Mr Semenyo, he has indicated he is no longer supportive of proceedings and the prosecution do not consider it is appropriate to compel him.

'In those circumstances we offer no further evidence in the case.' District Judge Mary Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty to the charge of racially aggravated behaviour.

Semenyo, who was a Bournemouth player at the time of the incident but later signed for Manchester City, had been due to give evidence last month but the trial was adjourned halfway through when Mr Mogan was taken to hospital after suffering a seizure.

The court had heard Mr Mogan, in a wheelchair, shouted at Semenyo as he went to take a throw-in about 30 minutes into the game.

Mark Mogan (right) has been found not guilty of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo (left) after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.

He was alleged to have stated: 'Hurry up and take the throw-in, you black b*****d.'.

Opening the case last month, Mr Jones noted: 'That racial abuse was shouted directly at Antoine Semenyo, who was close to him.

'Mr Semenyo briefly froze, as he couldn't believe what the male had noted.' Mr Mogan then shouted "I'm talking to you, you ****", the court heard.

Witnesses also mentioned they saw him throw his chewing gum at the footballer.

Semenyo reported the incident to the match referee and Mr Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time.

Mr Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police in interview that Semenyo had called him a cripple after he shouted at the player to 'hurry up'.

Mr Mogan, of Templehill Close in Dovecot, Liverpool, declined to comment as he left court.

Semenyo, who scored a brace in the game, had brought the incident to the attention of match referee Anthony Taylor and the match was briefly halted while both managers and captains were spoken to.

At half time an announcement was made to the crowd asking for no racist abuse and pictures on social media showed a man in a wheelchair being escorted along the touchline and out of the ground.

Mogan, pictured with Liverpool legend Robbie Fowler, would have been banned for life if he'd have been found guilty.

Merseyside Police later revealed the man had been arrested and then was bailed for three months pending further investigations.

Pictures on social media indicated Mogan playing wheelchair basketball for a team called the Greenbank Meteors while other images show him posing with Liverpool legends Robbie Fowler and Emile Heskey.

After he was charged, Liverpool confirmed he would be banned for life if found guilty but Judge Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty on Friday morning.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • St Mirren manager Craig McLeish claims self-interest and poor governance are killing Scottish football’s hopes of improvement.
  • McLeish is frustrated that Scottish Football Association chief football officer Craig Mulholland has reportedly had to dilute aims for young player quotas to appease five William Hill Premiership clubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 09:55 EST, 20 November 2026.

St Mirren manager Craig McLeish claims self-interest and poor governance are killing Scottish football’s hopes of improvement.

McLeish is frustrated that Scottish Football Association chief football officer Craig Mulholland has reportedly had to dilute aims for young player quotas to appease five William Hill Premiership clubs.

Mulholland was hoping to ensure teams featured Scotland Under-21 eligible players for an average of 60 minutes per league game and had two on the pitch for each cup tie.

McLeish mentioned: 'That’s damning that he’s having to change his looks to pander to clubs who aren’t really on board with it and don’t really have the best interests of the Scottish national team at heart.

'I understand why. We have owners from outwith this country. We have managers from outwith this country. They’re in jobs, they’re all fighting for their clubs.

'But why then are those people allowed to be the ones that hold the keys to the future of our country and the development of our national team?

St Mirren boss Craig McLeish believes self-interest at clubs is hampering Scottish football.

'It’s the way governance is set up and we’ve killed ourselves with that because the people who actually have a say in it have, not have no interest but they’ve got self-interest, and there’s a lot of self-interest at the top end.

Recent findings suggest that 'I just don’t see a way that we can really properly change unless something to do with governance changes and I just don’t ever see that happening. It’s really sad.'.

Although McLeish backs quotas, he fears that would not address the root cause of Scottish football’s problems.

'We always focus at the top end, what our league size is, quotas for young players, a national base,' mentioned the 36-year-old, who worked in St Mirren’s youth academy before his current role.

According to recent reports, 'We have a fundamental problem that starts at our youngest age groups, at four and five years of age, about how we actually teach kids to play. And until you fix that, you can’t fix the top end of it.

Recent findings suggest that 'It’s crazy some of the stuff that’s going on, the formats, how we teach kids. There’s just a massive lack of education and expertise at the very bottom of our pathway.

'In this country, football’s everyone’s sport and everyone gets access to it but if you take your young kids along to swimming or gymnastics or whatever other sport, you’re there with properly qualified coaches, teachers who have maybe done things at the top levels of that sport.

'We have nothing without the volunteers that work at the bottom end of the grassroots game, but they’re not teaching kids how to play football properly, in my mind.

'And you’re just hoping that they get put with a volunteer coach that can teach them something, that they get in with a really good group at the youngest ages.

Industry observers note that 'Because that development between the ages of three and eight, if you don’t get that right, you’re dead. You can’t do anything after that point, and we don’t do it well enough. And you’re just chasing yourself and we’ll never catch up.'.

The SFA has been contacted for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

According to recent reports, this was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”.

Sources indicate that asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso stated: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding newly introduced ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

Recent findings suggest that how different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Sources indicate that next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

Sources indicate that david Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Amazon rainforest plays a key part in the cycling of carbon and water on regional and global scales, and is widely viewed as a perennially evergreen ecosystem. However, writing in Nature, Song et al.1 report that there are extended periods when trees in most of the rainforest remain leafless. Known as deciduousness, this state occurs between the shedding of old leaves and the emergence and early development (flushing) of fresh ones. The authors also found that hydroclimatic conditions such as annual rainfall have a more crucial role in determining this pattern of leaf behaviour than do soil properties and light availability. The seasonal variation in tropical leaf cover and photosynthetic activity in the Amazon observed by the authors is less pronounced than that seen for broadleaf trees in temperate and boreal climate zones.

Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of new TV series' release

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour.".

The crowds revealed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

In a recent development, today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

Sources indicate that at first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

Sources indicate that but in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In a recent development, in an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

It has been revealed that the controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

It has been revealed that the "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

It has been revealed that despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been unveiled, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO states, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the fresh production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.

In a recent development, not for the first time, Mykhailo Mudryk was in a good position, and displayed poor judgement. This time, it was away from the pitch, in a two-hour, sit-down, tell-all interview involving gaffes galore.

Criticising London for its 20mph speed limit, saying 'it's hard to follow these rules, however much I'd like to' after his latest driving ban, and how the wealthy are taxed 45 per cent on these shores.

Naming 'Ukraine' when asked which is the best city in the world – he may have misunderstood the question, so we will let him off with that one – and admitting he signed contracts without reading them while denouncing the deals done by his former representatives.

It has been revealed that then there was his interviewer, a grinning chap called Dmitry Gordon, asking him if he speaks to his four cats in English, and why he wears earrings, and if girls send him pictures. Bizarre enquiries. Had Chelsea or Tottenham Hotspur known about this interview happening – and Daily Mail Sport understands they were not informed – then we cannot imagine either Premier League club would have liked such lines of questioning.

Nor will they, or their fanbases, be too fond of the 25-year-old Ukrainian explaining his move to England in the first place. He revealed how much he wanted to play for Arsenal, describing it as his 'dream' as he blamed his old agent for pushing him to Chelsea for the money.

What was supposed to be an opportunity for Mudryk to tell his side of the story, after a doping ban which cost him two years of his career, resembled more of a moany mess.

Mykhailo Mudryk's interview was a bizarre mess and indicated his utter naivety.

The Ukrainian winger was given a one-year driving ban in December last year.

By the end, the seriousness of his allegations against the Ukrainian national team with regard to his failed drugs test were softened by the nonsensical own goals much more likely to set social media alight.

Such as the naivety of a Chelsea player on loan at Tottenham appearing to pine for Arsenal, and saying he still wants to win the Ballon d'Or, which is only ever an admission prone to being patronised online even if a sign of his ambition.

Sources indicate that A reminder: Mudryk signed for Chelsea from Shakhtar Donetsk in January 2023 for £89million. He struggled, never looked like a winger worth such a fee. Frighteningly fast, but did not know how to use his weaponry properly in the Premier League. Graham Potter was his manager when he arrived. A few months later, it was Frank Lampard. A month after that, Mauricio Pochettino.

Then he was suspended for two years, during which time Chelsea supported his insistence that he was innocent and continued to pay his salary, believed to be worth around £100,000 per week.

While banned, he turned up in Wroclaw, Poland the day before the 2025 Conference League final, apparently there to collect his medal in case Chelsea won. Enzo Maresca was unaware, only learning that he was in the city when we told him at his pre-match press conference.

Upon Mudryk's return to football in the summer of 2026, Chelsea decided he needed to leave on loan, and another one of the Premier League's big-six sides gave him his second chance.

Sources indicate that tottenham called. Brentford, Brighton, Leeds and Coventry were among those also willing, but Roberto De Zerbi promised to give him a platform to prove his talents.

He appeared once, as a 74th-minute substitute away at Nottingham Forest in September. Then he disappeared, injured, and his only sighting since has been here, on YouTube, as a 'Guest of Gordon'.

Chelsea will also be unhappy about Mudryk's interview and were not informed about it.

Mykhailo Mudryk's is still two weeks away from a Tottenham return after a suffering setback to his recovery from an ankle injury.

Mudryk, who has played only 16 minutes since joining on loan from Chelsea, clashed with the Ukrainian FA this week when he blamed them for his positive drug test which ruled him out of football for almost two years.

He also risked the wrath of Spurs fans by admitting he only made the move across London to recover his fitness before returning to Stamford Bridge where Blues boss Xabi Alonso was 'counting on him'.

And he managed to annoy both Chelsea and Spurs fans by revealing, during the same YouTube interview, that he wanted to sign for Arsenal when he moved to the Premier League in January 2023 but his agent forced through the move with the best commission.

'I can understand the fans, but Mudryk is a good guy,' noted Spurs boss De Zerbi, who worked with the Ukraine international at Shakhtar Dontetsk and convinced him to resist interest from Brentford and Coventry and be reunited in North London.

Recent findings suggest that 'He's a good player. He suffered a lot for the situation in the last couple of years. He has just one thing to do, show on the pitch his qualities, show on the pitch that now he's playing for Tottenham. Tottenham is a major club, like the other clubs, not less at all.'.

Chelsea paid £86million for Mudryk but he made little impression before he was hit with a four-year ban in 2024, which was wiped out this summer enabling him to return to competition.

'He has no responsibility in this part,' remarked De Zerbi. 'Now his focus is just on the ball or just on the football. He has a substantial chance to play with us because Tottenham is a big club. He knows very well the coach, he knows very well the style of play.

Recent findings suggest that 'He knows I give him total confidence to show what he is. So to move the focus in the right direction, in a good direction. But I think he's working hard to recover and to play earlier.'.

Mudryk made his Spurs debut as a sub at Nottingham Forest in September but injured an ankle in training a few days later. He was initially expected to be out for two months with Saturday's game against Ipswich his target to return.

Sources indicate that 'The strategy was to be available for Ipswich or Sunderland,' stated De Zerbi, who will serve a touchline ban against Ipswich for three yellow cards. 'Then he felt not pain but he was not comfortable last week. And they take two weeks more, and step by step we're going to see the situation.'.

While there should be sympathy with Mudryk, who had to bite his tongue while banned and spending what he described as 'millions' on trying to clear his name, he made a poor choice in the platform chosen to finally speak up.

At one stage, he is asked bluntly whether he considered killing himself. 'No, that's not a way out,' he replied. The title of the video on YouTube, unhelpfully, mentions 'suicidal thoughts' regardless of his answer.

Mudryk may have thought it would help to talk so openly, especially to clarify those he holds responsible for the two years he lost as a footballer.

But he hardly endeared himself to his current club, Tottenham, or to his parent club, Chelsea, to whom he is still contracted into the 2030s.

He likened them to chaos, explaining: 'I came to a Chelsea that was, and perhaps still is, in the middle of a rebuild. It's not the Chelsea that existed under the previous owners, which was stable, had a clear system, coaches, without this constant galloping who knows where.'.

Such comments are unlikely to be well received when read by the club's hierarchy, while he also remarked on Chelsea's managerial merry-go-round: 'The coaches themselves don't know what tactics they'll play. They come to the club and try one set of tactics. Whether it works or not, they try another.'.

When Mudryk returns from his ankle injury, he will have to hope his football can do the talking. After this, neither Tottenham nor Chelsea are likely to want him to speak again any time soon.

Gold for the West Bank: Meet Palestinian karate champ Mariam Bsharat

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that "After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat stated.
  • It has been revealed that themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win.
  • "It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that "After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat stated. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome.".

It has been revealed that themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. In Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The 17-year-old won her second under-21 World Karate Championship gold medal competing for the Palestine national team in Poland in October.

"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.

Recent findings suggest that "I faced challenges in transportation," Bsharat remarked. "I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt ... which was very hard for me. And, financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed.".

Growing up in Nablus, Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.

"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," noted Bsharat, who competes in the division for fighters who weigh under 66 kilograms (145 pounds).

"I started it because my family was in that sport," Bsharat noted. "My father had a dojo, and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles — it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany, last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.

Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.

"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here," Bsharat said. "But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life, and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships.".

Recent findings suggest that as well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel, there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat stated, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” Bsharat stated.

"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag,” she said. "I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself.".

According to recent reports, that has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF). With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.

"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," the WKF wrote in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.

Should karate return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.

"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.

"But winning an Olympic medal, being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride.".

The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.

Published: 10:30 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:25 EST, 20 November 2026.

For anyone with anything resembling a retentive memory, the alarm bells were going off all over the shop on the day Sebastien Pocognoli was unveiled as the upcoming Scotland head coach.

Scottish Football Association (SFA) chief executive Ian Maxwell and chief football officer Craig Mulholland were there to crow about an extensive search of foreign fields to rival Captain Cook’s journeys around the Pacific and how data had helped land ‘one of Europe’s most sought-after coaches’ and secure the ‘aggressive, front-foot style of play’ that was going to bring a desired freshness.

In a recent development, it was impossible to avoid the elephant in the room, though. Two-and-a-half months earlier, ahead of the disaster zone that was the World Cup, they’d handed Steve Clarke a fresh four-year contract.

In a recent development, he was the polar opposite to Poco. Aggressive and front-foot, he most certainly wasn’t. The SFA knew Clarke didn’t have it in him to go for it at a major finals – as evidenced by two separate European Championship failures – but they decided to stick with the status quo anyway. Just as they did after Euro 2024, when he should have been sacked.

When Clarke finally did go of his own accord after the summer’s events in North America, Maxwell stated he was ‘sad’ the former Kilmarnock manager had stepped down and put a substantial dollop of blame on ‘some fairly hysterical commentary back home’.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland,  Pocognoli and SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell.

It just didn’t add up. How do you go from thinking a guy like Clarke is the future to tearing everything up, drafting in a London-based analytics firm to tell you who to go for as his replacement and coming up with a 39-year-old Belgian who wants to go for broke?

‘It doesn’t matter how you get there,’ offered Maxwell. ‘Let’s not get too hung up on the whys and the what-ifs.’.

Unfortunately, people are now starting to get hung up over the fact Pocognoli, for all the good on his CV, looks like he’s in the wrong movie – with his refusal to break from a failing three-at-the-back strategy suggesting a diploma from the Wilfried Nancy School of Intransigence ought to be on that resume too.

They are getting hung up on the fact captain Andy Robertson came out after the thrashing from Switzerland’s B-team to reveal the mood inside the camp has changed and warn there’s no breathing space to sort this out.

And they are getting hung up on the fact that it’s becoming considerably easier to reach the conclusion those above all of them at the very top of the SFA have never had a proper grip on things at all.

Clarke, of course, only exacerbated those concerns in September by expressing the view at a public event that Maxwell and Co ‘panicked a little bit’ in giving him that incomprehensible long-term deal because he’d threatened to announce he was quitting before the finals unless an agreement was reached.

Industry observers note that ‘I wanted to control my narrative,’ he explained. It was hard to know who emerged from those admissions looking worse.

Clarke’s off the plot now, though, and it’s Maxwell, Mulholland and the SFA president Mike Mulraney left to try and convince us all that there is some kind of rhyme or reason to it all.

Industry observers note that how things shape up with Pocognoli is an acid test for them. The rise or fall of a Scotland manager always hogs headlines. Yet, it is only one of a number of things coming together in what is starting to feel like a bit of a perfect storm.

Not so long ago, Maxwell and Mulholland were also yakking plenty about their statement project to increase game time for Scotland-eligible Under-21s.

It’s already in tatters, by the looks of things. The aims were watered down last month, without anything like the same fanfare, to involve Under-23 players and the intended votes on the proposals were pushed back.

A number of Premiership sides haven’t warmed to it and it remains to be seen whether it goes to a vote at all. Certainly, the radical change the top brass envisioned isn’t going to happen and that can only be regarded as an indicator that these guys running the game aren’t capable of taking it with them.

The start of Sebastien Pocognoli's reign has been concerning for Scotland fans.

Sources indicate that dundee manager Steven Pressley’s intervention over recent days hasn’t helped them either. After a long period on the outside looking in, Scotland have turned out in three major tournaments in the last five years.

According to recent reports, that has raised many millions of pounds, but the effect on elite level is questionable. Pressley talked of the sport being ‘built on sand’ as a result of there being no kind of national facility and you’d better believe it gained traction.

It has been revealed that ‘It states a lot about our strategy, our longevity and our long-term vision and we are finally seeing the effects of that. We have shown none of that over the period and it is all horribly catching up with us,’ he stated.

In a recent development, the SFA do own Hampden, of course, thanks to that peculiar £5million deal from 2019 that involved Willie Haughey and Sir Tom Hunter ponying up half the money. Yet, how distant those days of Maxwell talking about taking examples from the way VfB Stuttgart revamped the Mercedes-Benz Arena and potentially implementing them in Mount Florida seem now.

In a recent development, everyone appears to have given up on making the National Stadium better. Other problems have overtaken that old chestnut. Refereeing isn’t good enough. VAR isn’t up to scratch. General facilities require considerable improvement.

Should this Youth Initiative fail, there may also be a need for the SFA to look deeper within when addressing the dearth of top-tier talent coming through.

It has been revealed that it’s OK to blame clubs, but what about the level of coaching – and coach education – that exists at the national association? That’s before we even get to the ‘massive lack of expertise and education’ at the younger end of grassroots raised by St Mirren boss Craig McLeish.

According to recent reports, the SFA set-up for producing coaches was once the envy of many. We all remember Jose Mourinho and others at the Largs finishing school. Now? Even Maxwell, after stating there were no viable Scottish rivals to Pocognoli for the Scotland job, admitted the coaching pathway needs looked at.

There is only one problem here, though. Maxwell has been the chief executive since May 2018. He’s in his ninth year in the role. What has he really achieved? What have his big ideas been?

Recent findings suggest that yes, Scotland made it back to major finals under Clarke, but Clarke was a painfully obvious choice to be made national coach in 2019. He’d worked wonders at Rugby Park and did transfer that to the international scene until it came to actually turning out in those showpiece competitions.

Now they’ve had to get creative, there is so much hanging on Pocognoli’s reign for the guys at the top.

Recent findings suggest that maxwell was a bloke who landed in the role of Partick Thistle GM almost by mistake after failing to beat Jackie McNamara to the manager’s job. Just before leaving for the SFA, the Jags got relegated.

Talk of redeveloping Hampden has gone quiet as other problems take the spotlight.

At his Hampden unveiling, he had to fend off questions about only getting that position through behind-the-scenes politicking and insist he wouldn’t be a puppet for anyone.

Sources indicate that mulholland also seems a surprising choice as the architect of the national sport’s renovation. He spent two decades in the Rangers academy and eight years as head of it.

Has it been a conveyor belt of talent for the Ibrox first-team? Do you recall much wailing and gnashing of teeth when he left in 2023 amid a wider changing of the guard?

Then, there’s Mulraney, the former Alloa chairman and SFA director for over a decade.

Sources indicate that you don’t see much of him these days. Maybe because people want to ask about his position as chair of FIFA’s finance committee in the wake of the most greed-infested World Cup ever and the ongoing soap opera surrounding Gianni Infantino. But maybe not.

How things work out with Pocognoli might end up being the one thing that puts all these guys under the kind of examination that cannot be bodyswerved, but it’s only the tip of the iceberg.

What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one concern ranked above all others: the economy.
  • So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?
  • Recent findings suggest that markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one concern ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Recent findings suggest that markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

Recent findings suggest that with Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, mentioned in a note.

Sources indicate that "I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind.".

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

In a recent development, kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, stated the vote showed the extent of that opposition. Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of substantial tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

According to recent reports, "This election reveals that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he mentioned. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted.".

If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown stated, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

It has been revealed that that sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

Industry observers note that "Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office.".

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard noted, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump remarked in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election glitch — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

Sources indicate that "You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most notable thing now.".

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

It has been revealed that yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another problem vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the latest Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic challenges to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard remarked. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs.".

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

According to recent reports, but as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews stated. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”.

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

In a recent development, to play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

Industry observers note that it was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak stated. “I was waiting for my moment.”.

In a recent development, any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”.

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola noted they will now be out “for some time”.

Recent findings suggest that the loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

Sources indicate that the injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa stated: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”.

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

Sources indicate that however, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It has been revealed that but Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

Industry observers note that to play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”.

Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. In a recent development, breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be noted for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Published: 10:25 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:32 EST, 20 November 2026.

Manchester United CEO Omar Berrada insists the team got 'fundamentally better' after this summer's transfer window, as he warned ‘spending just for the sake of it’ is not the route to putting United back on top.

In his first sit-down interview in five months, Berrada tackled topics ranging from the relationship between the Glazers and Ineos, the imminent departure of youngster JJ Gabriel, the decision not to sign a left back in the summer, as well as the decision to push ahead for a new stadium despite supporter backlash on matchdays.

The United chief has been at the centre of furious protests and anti-ownership chanting at matches this season, alongside Director of Football Jason Wilcox, and he accepted that criticism of United's leadership has, mostly, been fair.

In an interview that aired shortly after new head coach Mauricio Pochettino spoke to the media for the first time, Berrada was pressed on how much accountability falls at his door with United heading to Anfield this weekend 18th in the Premier League table.

'I think if you think about the fact we've had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven't achieved the stability that we wanted, that's for sure,' Berrada told Sky Sports.

In a recent development, 'When it doesn't work out with the coach or the manager, we are all responsible. Myself, the football leadership, everyone who is involved around the coach and the staff and the players. We have to continue improving and getting better.

Manchester United's CEO Omar Berrada finally fronted up in an interview with Sky Sports.

Michael Carrick's sacking was yet another managerial change at United, with the hierarchy under massive scrutiny and Mauricio Pochettino now in the hotseat.

'There are different circumstances why it didn't work out with Erik [ten Hag], and Ruben [Amorim], and now Michael [Carrick], and we are always learning and, as I stated, trying to improve and understand what has failed.

'The challenge is we're trying to find the right manager for the squad that we have with a specific set of skills in that moment to make them perform at their best level.

It has been revealed that 'It's true, we have to accept the criticism that we haven't been able to achieve that stability with one coach and our aim is to do that as soon as possible. Of course, we hope now that Mauricio coming in will give us that stability that I think we all need.'.

Berrada's links to Manchester City, where he worked prior to joining United, were brought up, not least given he worked at the club during the period that City have had charges brought against them.

'I'm not concerned,' Berrada insisted.

But at his newly introduced home there are issues aplenty, not least having got another managerial appointment wrong, sacking Carrick less than six months after handing him a two-year deal, and so it was put to Berrada: is the club actually progressing?

'It's not good enough, not acceptable and that's why we've made the change that we made so that we can move forward,' he concluded.

(L-R) Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Berrada and Jason Wilcox have drawn plenty of ire from Man United fans.

'But we are laying the foundations for sustained growth, to put us in a position where we can be competitive consistently. It's not always been that.

'Last year we finished third, we were happy with the squad, we were happy with the way we were going. And now, a few months later, we are not where we need to be. But the foundations are there and I am convinced that we are heading in the right direction. Very positive.'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo remarked in a video on his Instagram account.

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world," Ronaldo remarked.

The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals — making him the men's record-holder for ⁠international ​appearances and for international goals.

He captained Portugal ​to their first major trophy at ​Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.

"It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not ​only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.

"If I ever made you happy, ​if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel ⁠proud ​of our country, then it ​was all worth it.".

He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people ​and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national ​team career.

The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7.".

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" it read.

The FPF intends to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much.".

While his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.

According to recent reports, ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp. He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.

Like Messi, Ronaldo intends to continue his club career with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that roughly 180 million people could be carrying previously unknown giant viruses inside their guts.
  • Large and giant viruses in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are a vast group of DNA viruses — some are so substantial that they can be seen under a light microscope — that mostly infect single-celled organisms in the environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many giant viruses can be seen under a light microscope.Credit: Gabrielle Voinot/Eurelios/Look at Sciences/SPL.

Industry observers note that roughly 180 million people could be carrying previously unknown giant viruses inside their guts. Microbiologists say that these ‘egoviruses’ could be the missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and distantly related poxviruses, such as those that cause smallpox and mpox, which can infect people and animals directly. The findings are published in Nature1.

Large and giant viruses in the phylum Nucleocytoviricota are a vast group of DNA viruses — some are so substantial that they can be seen under a light microscope — that mostly infect single-celled organisms in the environment.

Poxviruses are an outlier in the giant-virus world because they can directly infect humans and animals and their origin is a mystery, says Fasséli Coulibaly, a structural biologist at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia. Egoviruses could be the evolutionary bridge between microorganism-infecting giant viruses called asfuviruses and pathogenic poxviruses, he says.

Tom Delmont, a microbial ecologist at the French National Centre for Scientific Research in Paris, and his colleagues discovered egoviruses while combing through online libraries of metagenomes. These contain the genetic information of all the organisms in a particular environment, which means that researchers can hunt for microbes without having to cultivate them. When the team scanned for a single gene found in most nucleocytoviruses, they discovered egoviruses — the only type of nucleocytovirus that is prevalent in the gut.

According to recent reports, they found egovirus DNA in gut samples from people, buffalo, goats, chickens, deer and pigs. Six clades were unique to people. One of these clades is estimated to be present in roughly 1% of the global population, on the basis of the presence of at least one of two egovirus proteins in the samples they analysed.

The researchers detected these proteins in samples spanning a large proportion of the human population, from the Hadza, a hunter-gatherer group in Tanzania, to populations in Europe, the United States and South America, says Delmont. That suggests that egoviruses have been inhabiting the human gut for a long time, he adds.

That egoviruses are found in many animal species, including people, and are widespread around the world shows that giant viruses are more diverse than previously thought, states Subir Sarker, a molecular virologist at James Cook University in Townsville, Queensland. “This is a really groundbreaking study,” he adds.

In a recent development, to identify potential hosts for egoviruses in the gut, the team compared the amount of genetic overlap between egoviruses and organisms with a nucleus. The researchers found the most overlap with single-celled organisms that help ruminants, such as cows, to digest their food.

#37305. Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).
  • Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.
  • According to recent reports, by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

According to recent reports, by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a recent development, in a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd.".

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag.".

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka mentioned. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity.".

Koehler, though, is unconvinced.

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he noted. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system.".

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody.".

WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation.".

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place.".

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," remarked Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been.".

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

It has been revealed that in April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics.".

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.
